stem: In which year Vasco-da-Gama arrived at Calicut ?
expl: Vasco da Gama arrived at western coast port of Calicut on May 20, 1498 A.D. He discovered a new and alternative sea route to India and he was welcomed by Zamorin (Zamorin was the ancestral title of the rulers of Calicut), the then king of Calicut. The voyage of Vasco da Gama opened the new trade dimensions of the Indo-Portuguese (Europe) alliance. Vasco da Gama earned 60 times more profi t as compared to the cost of expeditions in Europe from black pepper trade with India, which encouraged other Portuguese traders. The Portuguese merchants established their commercial fi rms in India at the ports of Calicut, Goa, Daman, Diu and Hooghly. Francisco de Almeida came to India in 1505 AD as the fi rst Portuguese Viceroy. The ‘Blue Water’ policy is attributed to Francisco de Almeida, the fi rst Viceroy of Portuguese possessions in India. According to Blue water policy, “The Portuguese should be the sole trade power in the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean”. Portugese were the fi rst to build trade relation with India, among the European nations, who came by discovering new sea route to India. Albuquerque came to India in 1509 A.D. after him, as a new Viceroy. He annexed Goa in 1510 A.D.from Bijapur Adilshahi Sultanate. The Portuguese maintained Goa as the epicentre of their culture and entity.

stem: Who was the real founder of Portuguese power in India?
expl: The real founder of Portuguese power in India was Albuquerque (1509-15 A.D.). He established Portuguese State as a powerful regional power in India. The annexation of Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in November, 1510 was the fi rst signifi cant achievement of Albuquerque. The victory at Goa consolidated the Portuguese monopoly on the southern-western naval coast and established a regional Portuguese State in India. He encouraged Portuguese men to marry Indian women for enhancement of the Portuguese presence in India and the formation of permanent colonies.

With reference to the Captain Hawkins, which of the following statements is correct?
(1) He came to India in 1611 as an envoy of James-I.
(2) He was very well versed in Turkish language.
expl: William Hawkins sailed from the East India Company’s ship and reached to Surat in 1608 A.D. from Hector. After initial resistance from Portuguese, Hawkins arrived at the Mughal Court of Jahangir in Agra in April, 1609 A.D. Hawkins arrived at the Mughal Court with a letter signed by King James I of England, having introduction about Hawkins and the request of Mughal emperor’s favourable treatment for British traders. Therefore, Hawkins mission was a combination fo both, an imperial embassy and a commercial endeavour. He was sent by company, but with the credentials from the King, which made him representative of both– the King and the company, in the eyes of Mughal court. Hawkins was a good speaker of Turkish language. Jahangir was impressed by his knowledge of Turkish language and bestowed Hawkins, with the title of ‘English Khan’. Jahangir also granted Hawkins a mansab of 400. Therefore, statement (I) is false and the statement (II) is true.

expl: The First Carnatic War (1746-48 A.D.) was an offshoot of the Anglo-French rivalry in the Austrian War of succession that took place in Europe in 1740 AD. The British Commodore Bernett captured some French ships which became the immediate cause of the war. Nawab Anwaruddin sent an army under the command of Mahfooz Khan to besiege the French in Madras during the fi rst Carnatic War. The French Army (under the command of Captain Paradise) defeated Nawab’s Army at the Battle of St. Thome near Adyar river. Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (18 Oct, 1748 A.D.) ended the War of Austrian succession and with it fi rst Carnatic War ended and the Britishers reoccupied Madras. The fi rst Carnatic War is memorable for the War of St. Thome.

stem: What was the chief economic foundation of the triangular commerce between India, China and England?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: The triangular trade between India, China, and England in the 18th and 19th centuries was centered on opium. The British East India Company established their monopoly in the cultivation of opium in the region of Bengal and Bihar etc., they forced the farmers to cultivate opium and exported it to China, where it was in high demand despite government bans. Profi ts from the opium trade were used to purchase Chinese goods like tea, silk, and porcelain for England, while manufactured goods from England were exported to India, completing the trade cycle. This exploitative system had severe social and economic consequences, including the Opium Wars between Britain and China. While commodities like silk and black pepper were also traded, opium was the chief economic foundation of this triangular commerce.
